prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit.

We represent: defendant employer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that temporal proximity alone, absent unusually suggestive timing, is insufficient to establish causation for a retaliation claim.

Cite at least six decisions of the Third Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## II. TEMPORAL PROXIMITY ALONE, ABSENT UNUSUALLY SUGGESTIVE TIMING, CANNOT ESTABLISH CAUSATION

A retaliation plaintiff must show a causal connection between protected activity and the challenged action. *Moore v. City of Philadelphia*, 461 F.3d 331, 340–41 (3d Cir. 2006). That burden is not met by pointing to the sequence of events. Under Title VII's retaliation provision, the plaintiff must ultimately prove that the protected activity was the but-for cause of the adverse action. *Univ. of Tex. Sw. Med. Ctr. v. Nassar*, 570 U.S. 338, 360 (2013). Treating timing alone as proof of causation would collapse that standard into the fallacy of *post hoc, ergo propter hoc*.

This Court has therefore long held that timing supports an inference of causation by itself only when it is "unusually suggestive" of retaliatory motive. *Krouse v. Am. Sterilizer Co.*, 126 F.3d 494, 503 (3d Cir. 1997); *Williams v. Phila. Hous. Auth. Police Dep't*, 380 F.3d 751, 760 (3d Cir. 2004). The inquiry is not satisfied by a showing that one event followed another. In *Farrell v. Planters Lifesavers Co.*, 206 F.3d 271, 279–81 (3d Cir. 2000), the Court explained that where the interval is not so close as to be unduly suggestive, a plaintiff must point to additional evidence, such as intervening antagonism or inconsistencies in the employer's explanation, that, viewed as a whole, supports an inference of a causal link. *Accord Shellenberger v. Summit Bancorp, Inc.*, 318 F.3d 183, 189–90 (3d Cir. 2003).

The Court has applied this rule with discipline. In *LeBoon v. Lancaster Jewish Community Center Ass'n*, 503 F.3d 217, 232–33 (3d Cir. 2007), it held that a gap of three months between the protected activity and the adverse action, without more, cannot create an inference of causation. Likewise, in *Williams*, 380 F.3d at 760, the Court distinguished the very short intervals found sufficient in earlier cases from intervals too long to carry the inference alone. *See also Fasold v. Justice*, 409 F.3d 178, 189–90 (3d Cir. 2005) (declining to infer causation from timing where the interval was not unusually suggestive and the record lacked other evidence of a link); *Marra v. Phila. Hous. Auth.*, 497 F.3d 286, 302 (3d Cir. 2007) (looking to the record as a whole when timing alone does not establish causation); *Daniels v. Sch. Dist. of Phila.*, 776 F.3d 181, 196 (3d Cir. 2015) (same framework). These decisions draw the same line. Timing that is immediate and striking may suffice, but anything less requires independent evidence of retaliatory motive.

The Supreme Court's decision in *Clark County School District v. Breeden*, 532 U.S. 268, 273–74 (2001) (per curiam), reinforces the point. There, the Court observed that temporal proximity can support an inference of causation only when the events are "very close" in time, and it rejected reliance on a lengthy gap. It also noted that employers need not suspend previously planned actions upon learning of protected activity. *Id.* at 272. That principle matters here. An employer that was already pursuing a course of action before the protected activity cannot be said to have retaliated merely because the action was completed afterward.

Applying these principles, Plaintiff cannot carry her burden on timing alone. The interval between her protected activity on [date] and the [adverse action] on [date] was [__] [days/weeks/months] (App. [__]). That interval is far removed from the immediate, unusually suggestive timing this Court has found sufficient. It is also comparable to, or longer than, intervals this Court has held insufficient as a matter of law. *LeBoon*, 503 F.3d at 233.

Because timing does not carry the inference, Plaintiff must identify other record evidence showing a causal link. *Farrell*, 206 F.3d at 280–81. She has none. The record shows no pattern of antagonism following her protected activity, and it shows no inconsistency in the reasons Defendant has given for its decision. Instead, it shows that [the legitimate, non-retaliatory basis for the decision] preceded or was independent of the protected activity (App. [__]). Without such evidence, the claim rests on the bare sequence of events, which is the inference this Court has repeatedly refused to draw.

This Court should hold that Plaintiff failed to establish causation and affirm.
